reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: The contact quality is elite and the discipline is quietly serious. A 93.1 mph average exit velocity sits in the 96th percentile, and a 11.7% walk rate pairs with an 18.3% strikeout rate that most sluggers his age would envy. The .365 xwOBA and .495 xSLG say the projection's 43 home runs across a full 702-PA season aren't a reach, they're what happens when you hit the ball that hard and take enough pitches to stay in favorable counts. The one drag on the profile is the glove, where his OAA percentile sits at 1, meaning if Tampa moves him off third base the offensive bar rises because he'll need a corner that forgives the defense.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The xwOBA splits tell the whole two-way story: .407 as a hitter, .257 as a pitcher, both sitting in the 94th percentile or higher. That kind of profile doesn't have a comp because there isn't one. The bat carries a 16.4% barrel rate and 13.5% walk rate into a projected .935 OPS over 693 plate appearances, while the 30.6% whiff rate against him as a hitter is the one soft spot, the place pitchers fish and occasionally land. On the mound, a 2.72 xERA and 98.1 mph fastball with 2488 rpm of spin give him genuine front-of-rotation stuff, and the 27.9% strikeout rate backs that up, even if the 7.6% walk rate keeps the profile from being truly clean. The honest ceiling here isn't a category or a comp, it's a player who posts MVP-caliber offense and ace-caliber pitching in the same season, and the floor, if the elbow holds, is still a .900-plus hitter who changes a lineup by himself.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact profile has always been the catch: 92.4 mph average exit velocity, a 13.6% barrel rate, .485 xSLG, the raw power grades out as genuine and consistent, and yet a 35.6% chase rate and 30.7% whiff rate that keep the ceiling perpetually in debate. What the Statcast profile says is that Walker hits the ball harder than almost everyone when he does connect, and the projection trusts that enough to land on .280/.340/.491 with 31 home runs across a full 672 PA season. The stolen base projection at 21 is credible given 29.2 ft/s sprint speed; he has the legs to make noise on the bases even when the strikeout rate costs him at-bats. Everything hinges on whether the chase discipline stabilizes, because if it doesn't, the .353 xwOBA stays a beautiful number he never quite reaches.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .474 and the barrel rate at 13.1%, a pairing that explains how a 22-year-old projects to 33 home runs and a .803 OPS across 700 plate appearances. That's a legitimate middle-of-the-order profile, and at his age the floor hasn't hardened yet. reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. Edwards chases just 24.2% of pitches and whiffs at a 16.8% clip, which puts him in genuinely rare company for a middle infielder, and that discipline is the reason a .285 AVG with an .363 OBP is believable across a full season. The power ceiling is the honest ceiling: 86.9 mph average exit velocity and a 3.3% barrel rate mean the projection's 7 home runs aren't a floor, they're about the top of the range. What he actually is, if the bat-to-ball skills hold, is a high-OBP, high-speed up-the-middle regular, the kind who runs his way to value with 23 stolen bases while the slugging line (.381 projected) stays quiet.

reports.name: George Kirby
reports.published_report: The whole profile comes down to one trade: he almost never walks anyone, and hitters make a lot of contact. A 5.5% walk rate puts him in the top tier of MLB starters for command, and a 35.0% chase rate means batters are regularly chasing his stuff out of the zone, but a 22.4% whiff rate says they're making contact when they do swing, which is why the strikeout rate sits at a below-average 20.4%. The result is a pitcher whose xERA of 3.88 and xwOBA of .305 land at roughly league average, held together entirely by his ability to limit free passes and generate weak contact rather than dominate at-bats. If the chase rate softens or his hard-hit rate climbs from 41.2%, the profile has nowhere to hide, and he's a back-end starter with a very specific skill keeping him functional, not a guy with a margin of error.

reports.name: Willi Castro
reports.published_report: The actual-batting profile here is propped up by a .260 average floating well above a .234 xBA, and that gap tends to close. A 37.3% chase rate and 30.5% whiff rate pair with an 87.7 mph average exit velocity to explain why the .310 xwOBA sits in the bottom third of the league, and none of those levers are easy to fix at 29. The projection still sees a useful player, but "sees" is the wrong word: if the underlying contact quality stays where it is, what you get is a multi-tool piece carrying 18 projected home runs and 11 steals whose counting stats owe something to Coors. The profile hinges on Colorado's park doing work that a 22nd-percentile xBA simply cannot.

reports.name: Oneil Cruz

The bat makes elite contact when it connects, and an 11.1% walk rate gives him enough margin that the projection lands at .341 OBP despite the strikeouts. reports.name: Bryson Stott
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at the 80th percentile while xSLG lands right at the median — that gap defines what Stott is: a contact-quality hitter whose bat-to-ball skill is genuinely above average, but whose raw power keeps him from being more than a solid regular. His 19.0% whiff rate grades at the 79th percentile, which is the foundation; he doesn't give away many swings, and the 16.9% strikeout rate follows from that. The projection fills out the profile honestly, a .337 OBP with 27 steals and 11 home runs across 594 PA, a second baseman who beats you with on-base and legs rather than anything loud off the bat. If the 96th-percentile fielding (OAA) holds at second, Philadelphia has a genuine two-way asset; if the 89.2 mph average exit velocity represents a ceiling rather than a floor, the projected .406 SLG is close to what he'll always be.

reports.name: Hunter Brown
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument. Brown's 13.7% BB% sits at the 4th percentile, nearly every qualified starter issues fewer free passes, and that single number is doing damage across a Statcast profile that's otherwise quietly functional: a 3.78 xERA, an 85.7 mph average exit velocity at the 97th percentile, contact quality that's genuinely suppressed even when he misses the zone too often. The strikeouts are real enough at 24.1%, the barrel rate is clean at 6.3%, and the projection lands at a 3.57 ERA over 106.4 innings, which is a useful rotation piece, but that workload estimate itself tells you the system doesn't fully trust him to stay efficient through a full year. If the walk rate tightens, the exit velocity profile supports a mid-rotation workhorse worth building around; if it doesn't, he's a backend starter with a beautiful contact-suppression trick and a self-inflicted ceiling.

reports.name: Mickey Moniak
reports.published_report: The .506 projected SLG is the number that needs explaining, and the Statcast profile explains it only halfway. Contact quality is genuinely mid-tier, with a 10.0% barrel rate and 41.9% hard-hit rate sitting right around average, but the xSLG of .400 in the current MLB line is a 50th-percentile outcome, not a 25-homer profile. Coors is doing real work here. The deeper problem is the chase rate, 41.5% in the current MLB line at the 4th percentile, which pairs with a 5.6% walk rate to produce an OBP that the projection has at .296, and that's the ceiling on his floor, not a number with much room to grow. If the park factor compresses or the plate discipline doesn't improve, you're left with a pull-side power bat who strikes out 26.3% of the time and can't get on base, which is a bench outfielder, not an everyday one.

reports.name: Ryan Sloan

His strikeout stuff is fine, 111 punchouts and 11.5 per nine at the level translating to roughly league-average swing-and-miss in the majors, but the command is the separator, sitting at the 99th percentile among pitchers in this pool. If the stuff holds its shape as he climbs, you're looking at a back-end starter who doesn't beat himself; if the velo or movement flattens out in the upper minors, the floor is depth arm and the walk rate becomes context rather than a calling card.

That tension defines what Cease is right now — a true swing-and-miss weapon who gives back a portion of his damage by not throwing enough strikes. reports.name: Luke Keaschall

Keaschall's 22.2% chase rate and 15.4% strikeout rate sit well above the league median, and at 28.8 ft/s he's a real baserunning weapon, but 85.3 mph average exit velocity and a 3.7% barrel rate describe a hitter who makes contact with the ball rather than to it. The projection's .269/.358/.381 is exactly what the Statcast profile predicts: a patient, speedy, light-power second baseman whose value lives in the OBP line and the stolen base column. Everything here works if the contact quality holds where it is and the walks stay near 9.6%, but if pitchers learn to attack him early and the chase rate creeps up, there's not enough thump in the profile to stay useful. Low-end everyday player on a good day, a useful bench piece if it doesn't hold.

At 13.1%, Reynolds draws walks at a rate that puts him in rarefied company, and it's what elevates a .249 xBA into a .350 xwOBA — the bat-to-ball isn't carrying him, the plate discipline is. His 46.4% hard-hit rate and a 25.1% chase rate confirm the contact that does land tends to land well, even if the 28.9% whiff rate suggests he sells out occasionally when pitchers do get him to expand. The projection settling at .365 OBP with 18 home runs across 702 PA is exactly what this looks like on paper: a patient, above-average everyday outfielder whose floor is defined by whether that walk rate holds at the big-league level, because if pitchers start attacking the zone more aggressively and the whiff rate climbs, the xBA has nowhere to go.

reports.name: Zebby Matthews
reports.published_report: That 11.2% barrel rate is the number that defines him, sitting at the 5th percentile among pitchers — hitters aren't just making contact, they're squaring him up. The fastball at 95.2 mph is fine, but a 22.7% whiff rate and 28.0% chase rate that both sit near the bottom third of the league mean he isn't missing bats often enough to compensate for what happens when contact lands. Walk rate at 7.3% is genuinely passable, which keeps the floor from collapsing entirely, and 126.6 projected innings suggests Minnesota sees a rotation piece rather than pure relief depth. If he can't suppress hard contact more reliably, a 4.56 xERA says the ERA will live in uncomfortable territory regardless of how the surface numbers occasionally flatter him.

reports.name: Brandon Lowe
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the power metrics tell completely different stories, and the 32 projected home runs are only believable if you start with the power side. At 91.1 mph average exit velocity with an 11.9% barrel rate and 46.0% hard-hit rate, the bat genuinely gets to loud contact, and that .424 xSLG reflects a real quality-of-contact profile. The problem is a 35.2% whiff rate sitting at the 4th percentile, paired with a 33.7% chase rate, which is how a hitter posts a .235 xBA while also posting a .321 xwOBA: he hits the ball hard when he hits it, and misses a lot. The projection's .247/.315/.464 line holds if you believe the hard contact keeps outrunning the strikeouts, and the barrel rate gives you reasonable cause to think it can, but if the whiff rate climbs further or the barrel rate dips, the batting average gets ugly fast and the power number shrinks with it.

reports.name: Nasim Nuñez
reports.published_report:
The Statcast contact profile is brutal: 0.3% barrel rate, 85.1 mph average exit velocity, and an xSLG of .269 that lands at the first percentile, and the projection follows the evidence straight to a .556 OPS over 520 plate appearances. Two projected home runs in a near-full season. That's not a hitter, that's a roster slot being asked to do hitting.

What keeps him employable is 29.7 ft/s sprint speed at the 97th percentile, paired with 49 projected stolen bases and a 10.2% walk rate that at least gives the legs something to work with. The contact metrics have no floor to fall through; the discipline and speed do the carrying. If the speed ages or the walk rate erodes, there's nothing left, because the bat has never been and isn't becoming the thing here — he's a borderline regular whose value lives entirely in what he does between the bases and in the field.

reports.name: Davis Martin
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile tells an uncomfortable story: a 4.71 xERA with a .333 xwOBA, both sitting in the 24th percentile, while a 44.4% hard-hit rate ranks in the 8th. The chase rate is legitimately interesting at 32.3%, and the 2412 rpm fastball spin gives him a weapon, but hitters who do connect are doing real damage, and a 20.9% strikeout rate isn't enough to paper over that contact quality. ValuCast's projection of a 4.32 ERA over 148.5 innings is essentially the optimistic read, banking on that chase rate and barrel suppression (6.8%) holding while the hard-hit numbers regress toward something survivable. If they don't, this is a back-end arm on a rebuilding White Sox staff who runs out of rope before the season does.

reports.name: Emil Morales
reports.published_report: The power is doing something loud at 19, and the question is whether it survives the climb. Across A+ & A in 2026, Morales is slashing .295/.383/.546 with 24 home runs and a .251 ISO in 506 plate appearances, numbers that rank in the 94th and 96th percentiles among his hitter pool for power and slug. The MLB-equivalent translation on the ISO lands at .16, barely above league average, which tells you how much of the current thump is level-driven, and his strikeout rate already translates to 29.8% against a world where 22.0% is ordinary. If the bat stays disciplined enough to keep those 59 walks alive against better stuff, you're talking about a real middle-of-the-order profile at short; if the strikeouts calcify, this is a right-handed bench piece who ages into a corner spot.

His 19% K rate in the minors translates to 21.5% against major league pitching, his walk rate comes out at 8.2%, and his ISO lands at .150, which is exactly league average. What plays at the upper minors as a genuine hit tool reads, in MLB context, as a contact-first profile with no separator. If the contact rate holds at the highest level, he's a useful bench bat who plays second base and gets on base; if pitchers find the hole the K rate hints exists, the floor is depth.

reports.name: Jonah Tong
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument here. Tong's 5.1 BB/9 at AAA translates to 4.7 against MLB hitters, which is nearly a run and a half per nine above what the average big-league starter allows in free passes. The strikeout stuff is legitimate, 118 punchouts across 100 innings at AAA and a K/9 that converts to 9.1 in MLB context, but a K-BB% that would sit below league average at the top level tells you the strikeouts aren't happening fast enough to cover the damage the walks create. If the command ever sharpens, there's a back-end arm here; if it doesn't, what's left is a depth piece who runs deep counts, stresses bullpens, and loses the margins that define a rotation spot.

reports.name: Michael King
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile and the projection are telling two very different stories, and that gap is the whole read. His xERA sits at 4.28 with a 21.2% strikeout rate and 9.4% walk rate, nothing that screams top-of-rotation, yet the projection has him at a 3.38 ERA over 186.9 innings. What bridges that gap is contact quality: hitters are barreling him at just 8.4% and averaging 86.8 mph exit velocity, both translating to soft, manageable contact despite the pedestrian swing-and-miss numbers. The underlying Statcast rates say he's been getting away with mediocre stuff by suppressing damage, and if that contact management holds across a full starter's workload, the 3.38 is reachable, but if hitters start squaring him up more consistently, the xERA is closer to his real floor.

reports.name: Abner Uribe
reports.published_report: The barrel rate tells the story here: 1.6%, a perfect 100th-percentile mark, backed by a 97.9 mph fastball that hitters simply cannot elevate. Uribe's xwOBA sits at .260 and his xERA at 2.78, both in the 93rd percentile, so the 2.28 ERA in the projection isn't wishful — the contact suppression is that severe. The walk rate, 9.4%, is the one live wire; his chase rate of 27.9% is below average, which means he's getting outs through pure stuff rather than command, and when the stuff catches too much of the zone he pays for it. If he tightens the zone at all, he's a high-leverage weapon Milwaukee can deploy in any situation; if he doesn't, he stays exactly what the projection says, 20 holds, 7 saves, and an ERA that flatters a profile held together by one extraordinary quality.

reports.name: Owen Caissie

The contact is genuinely punishing when it happens, with 91.2 mph average exit velocity and 45.7% hard-hit rate, but a whiff rate at the 4th percentile means the bat rarely finds the ball, and his .212 xBA reflects that brutally. The power translates to something in the .407 xSLG, but the .302 xwOBA lands at the 24th percentile because the strikeouts swallow the margin. reports.name: Melvin Hernandez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument here. At A-ball last season, Melvin Hernandez issued 1.6 walks per nine over 121.7 innings, and the MLB-equivalent translation comes out to 2.4 BB/9, comfortably below what most big-league starters allow. The strikeout picture is the honest tension: 7.2 K/9 at A translates to 5.9 at the MLB level, and the MLB-average sits at 8.6, so the ceiling is built on command, not swing-and-miss. If he holds that walk rate as competition sharpens, a multi-inning or setup role is plausible; if the strikeouts never develop, you're looking at a depth arm's worth of profile.

reports.name: Matt Wilkinson
reports.published_report: The profile is built on command, not stuff. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Wilkinson's 1.0 WHIP ranks at the 96th percentile among pitchers with 20-plus innings, and his walk rate sits at the 84th, but the strikeout number translates to an 8.3 K/9 at the MLB level, barely a tick below where MLB starters average. The 92 strikeouts over 87 innings look fine until you realize the margin for error is thin: if hitters catch up to him and contact quality ticks up, the walk rate that currently reads as an asset becomes exposure instead. Floor and ceiling land in the same place here, a depth arm who misses just enough bats to rotate through a staff without embarrassing himself.

reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing working in his favor right now. Across 36 innings at AAA, Wells has posted a 2.8 BB/9, and that control profile translates to roughly league-average territory at the MLB level, 3.1 against 3.2, which is genuinely the cleanest part of what is otherwise a thin case. The strikeout rate doesn't carry its weight: 9.0 K/9 at AAA translates to 8.3, a tick below what the league puts up, and a K-BB% of 16% in the minors becomes 13.1% in MLB context, again just shy of average. Eight starts is not enough to trust any of it firmly, and if the command slips even modestly, there's not enough swing-and-miss to compensate. The ceiling here is a depth arm; the floor is a depth arm.

reports.published_report: The surface numbers at AA are genuinely loud: .309/.395/.565 with 48 stolen bases and 15 home runs across 282 plate appearances, and the percentile pool rates his OPS and slugging at 97. Then you run the translation and the BABIP is .430. That's the whole problem — a contact profile running this hot on balls in play, paired with a strikeout rate that translates to 30.4% at the MLB level, means you're betting the batting average holds when the luck normalizes. If it doesn't, the ISO translates to .176, the walk rate lands at 9.0%, and you're left with a bench profile that runs well. The speed and the raw power are both present, but until the strikeout-BABIP combination sorts itself out at a higher level, this is a lottery ticket with a bench bat as the floor.

reports.name: Brady Smith
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and the translation is where it gets complicated. Across A+ & A, Brady Smith is punching out hitters at 13.2 per nine over 80.7 innings, 118 strikeouts against 34 walks, and that K-BB% sits in the 94th percentile of the pitcher pool. The problem is that when you run the MLB-equivalent translation, the strikeouts flatten to 8.7 per nine, essentially league average, and the walks translate to 4.2 against a translated K-BB% of 13.1 percent where the MLB average sits at 13.5, meaning the dominant shape at the lower levels becomes a break-even profile one level at a time. The whole case hinges on whether the swing-and-miss travels up the ladder or belongs to the level.

reports.name: Yamal Encarnacion
reports.published_report: The stolen bases carry this profile. Forty-eight at AA across 395 plate appearances is a legitimate weapon, and the 18 K% at that level translates to 21.3% in the majors, right at the 22.0% MLB average, meaning the contact ability that makes the speed playable should survive the climb. The power doesn't travel: a .117 ISO at AA becomes .11 in an MLB context, and the average sits at .15. If the legs and bat-to-ball hold, he's a bench bat who can change a game on the bases; if the speed diminishes even a little, what's left is a second baseman without enough thump to force regular playing time.

reports.name: Ben Kudrna
reports.published_report:
Two innings. That's the entire current AAA sample, and it's doing almost no work here.

What the translation shows isn't alarming but isn't encouraging: a K/9 that matches the MLB average exactly at 8.6, a BB/9 of 3.8 where the average sits at 3.2, and a K-BB% of 12.4 when the typical MLB starter lands at 13.5. If the strikeout rate doesn't climb and the walks stay where they are, the profile resolves as a depth arm, which is exactly where the ceiling lands anyway. The honest read here is that 2.0 IP can't tell you much, and ValuCast's rankings reflect that uncertainty, sliding him six spots in three days.

reports.name: Wilson Rodriguez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is loud for a 21-year-old at A+: 58 walks across 364 plate appearances, with a translated BB% of 11.4 against a big-league pool that averages 8.5. That's the selling point. The power doesn't come with it — an ISO of .167 at A+ translates to .127 in the majors, meaningfully short of the 8.5 average, and the 20 stolen bases show he knows he has to manufacture something when he does get on. If the plate discipline holds as he climbs and the raw pop develops enough to punish pitchers for nibbling, there's a fringe regular in here; if the power stays where it is, he's a bench piece with a useful OBP, and the ceiling note in the data says the system agrees.
